## Treatment, at the level of principle

The mainstay for urticaria is a non-sedating H1-antihistamine, with national guidance describing
up-titration beyond the standard licensed amount under specialist advice where the response is
inadequate — the specific multiples, the licensing position and who may do it are
**country-dependent** and are in your national guidance and formulary, not here. [consensus] The
older sedating antihistamines are generally avoided for maintenance because of their effects on
sleep architecture, cognition and driving. [consensus] Long-term systemic corticosteroids are not
a treatment for chronic urticaria; a short course has a place in a severe flare in some guidance.
[consensus] Beyond that there are specialist escalations, including an anti-IgE monoclonal
antibody and immunosuppressants, with availability and funding differing by country.
[country-dependent]

For bradykinin-mediated angioedema the principle is the opposite of escalation: identify the
pathway, stop the responsible drug where there is one, and use a pathway-specific treatment
through a service that holds a plan for that person.

## The human stakes, said plainly

No analogy in this section.

**Anaphylaxis is the emergency and it is defined by what is happening beyond the skin.** Urticaria
with any of airway compromise, difficulty breathing, wheeze, stridor, hoarseness, tongue or throat
swelling, a sense of the throat closing, collapse, or low blood pressure is anaphylaxis until
proven otherwise, and the response is immediate adrenaline given by someone trained to give it,
emergency services, and nothing that delays either. Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line
treatment for anaphylaxis in every mainstream guideline and antihistamines are not a substitute
for it. [consensus] **The doses and the devices are in your resuscitation council's guidance and
your formulary, and they are not in this answer.** Skin signs can be absent in anaphylaxis, which
is why their absence does not exclude it.

**Laryngeal angioedema is an airway emergency whichever pathway caused it**, and in the
bradykinin-mediated forms the drugs that work for anaphylaxis will not reverse it, so the airway
has to be secured and a pathway-specific treatment given. People with hereditary C1 inhibitor
deficiency are usually given written plans and medication to carry, and that plan is the authority
in an attack.

**And the chronic disease is not trivial.** Chronic urticaria is itchy day and night, disrupts
sleep, is visible, and is frequently dismissed as a rash. People commonly arrive having eliminated
most of their diet on the basis of a test result that never meant what they were told it meant,
and part of the consultation is undoing that. Angioedema of the face does not look like a minor
problem to the person who has it or to anyone who sees them. None of that is written here to be
affecting; it is written because it changes what the consultation has to contain.

Without softening: nothing here is for any reader's own use and no treatment named here is a
recommendation. Anyone with swelling of the lips, tongue, mouth or throat, any difficulty
breathing or swallowing, a hoarse voice with swelling, or a feeling that the throat is closing,
needs emergency help immediately — call your local emergency number. Anyone with recurrent
swelling without weals, or with unexplained recurrent abdominal pain and swellings, needs
assessment for the bradykinin-mediated causes rather than more antihistamine.

## What an examiner digs into next

How long one weal lasts, and what it means if a lesion is still there the next day. Why the itch,
the redness and the swelling arrive together. Why extensive allergy testing in chronic spontaneous
urticaria is unhelpful. The difference between an aggravating factor and a cause. Where the
six-week line is drawn and what it separates. Why the inducible urticarias are the ones a bedside
test settles. The single most useful question in distinguishing the two angioedema pathways. Why
an antihistamine fails against bradykinin-mediated angioedema, phrased as mechanism rather than as
dose. Why the first attack on an ACE inhibitor can be years after starting it. And what makes a
presentation anaphylaxis rather than urticaria.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

The standing documents for this specialty are listed in
[`../../../for-agents/SOURCES-dermatology.md`](../../../for-agents/SOURCES-dermatology.md),
and they are the authority for everything procedural or quantitative here. Specific to this
answer:

  up-titration of antihistamine: the urticaria guidance used where you practise — an international
  consensus guideline exists and is widely adopted, and national bodies issue their own versions
  that differ in the detail. Yours is the authority.
* For anaphylaxis — recognition, the drug, the route, the doses, the devices and the follow-up:
  your national resuscitation council's guidance and your national formulary. This answer
  deliberately contains no dose.
* For hereditary and acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency — diagnosis, the specific treatments,
  prophylaxis and the individual action plan: your national immunology or specialist angioedema
  service, which is where these patients are managed and where the plan lives.
* For any medicine named or implied, including the antihistamines, the anti-IgE monoclonal
  antibody and the angioedema-specific agents: your national formulary, for licensing,
  availability and dosing.
* For drug-induced angioedema and drug causes of urticaria: your national formulary's adverse
  effect entries, and this domain's m054 for the drug eruption reasoning.
* For urticarial vasculitis and the autoinflammatory syndromes: a current standard textbook of
  dermatology, and your national rheumatology or immunology pathway.

Revision material for someone already training in or qualified for the field. Not a clinical
reference, not a decision aid, and not reviewed by a clinician. It is not for use in making a
decision about anyone's care, including your own.

**No dose, agent, device, up-titration multiple or treatment schedule appears in this answer, and
none of it addresses any reader's own treatment.** The absence of the adrenaline dose is
deliberate: anaphylaxis treatment is set by your resuscitation council and your formulary, the
figures differ by age and by device, and a number quoted here without its document would be
dangerous rather than helpful.

with swelling, stridor, collapse, or a feeling that the throat is closing, is a medical emergency
— call your local emergency number. Someone with a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector and an
individual action plan should follow that plan, which was written for them and which overrides
anything general.

Local guidance and the policy where you practise are the authority on all of this, and they differ
by country and by institution.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The mechanisms and the discrimination between the two angioedema pathways are settled, and they
are the part worth memorising. What moves is the treatment ladder. The internationally adopted
urticaria guideline has been revised several times and the position on up-titration, on the
sequencing of specialist agents and on the role of short corticosteroid courses has changed
between revisions, so the edition matters. Several newer agents acting on mast cell signalling
have been in late-stage development for chronic spontaneous urticaria and the licensed landscape
is likely to look different within a few years. In hereditary angioedema the treatment options
have expanded substantially over the last decade, including long-term prophylaxis given by
different routes, and access to them varies sharply by country. The understanding of chronic
spontaneous urticaria as substantially autoimmune has strengthened rather than reversed. Current
as of October 2026.

and it makes no rain. Where the six-week line falls. Why the inducible urticarias are the ones a
bedside test settles — the effect is in the move's own data. The single most useful question
separating the two angioedema pathways. Why an antihistamine fails against bradykinin-mediated
angioedema, phrased as mechanism and not as dose. Why the first attack on an ACE inhibitor can be
years after starting it. And what makes a presentation anaphylaxis rather than urticaria.

written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not

* For drug-induced angioedema and drug causes of urticaria: your national formulary's adverse

# A working drug selects for the cells it cannot kill, and the route of escape names the next move

A targeted agent is given because the tumour carries a specific molecular lesion the agent acts
on. Where the lesion is a genuine dependency, the response can be fast and deep. In advanced
disease it almost always ends.

The ending is the part worth understanding, because the usual explanations are wrong. The drug has
not worn off. The dose has not become incorrect. What has changed is the **population being
treated**, and the treatment is part of what changed it. So the useful question at progression is
not *whether* the drug stopped working but *how* — because the escape routes fall into a small
number of classes, and each class implies a different next step. One class is answered by another
drug against the same target. One is answered only by blocking two things at once. One is answered
by abandoning the target altogether. One is not a biology problem at all.

No gene, drug or disease is named in this answer, deliberately. The classes are the teachable
content; the examples date within a year or two, and naming them here would invite a reader to
treat a revision note as a current list.

Each load-bearing claim below is marked with the kind of thing it is: **mechanism** (derivable
from how the biology works), **definitional** (true because a classification says so),
**consensus** (widely agreed professional practice), or **country-dependent** (varies by nation,
region or institution, and changes).

## The four routes out, and what each one implies

```
   WHAT THE DRUG NEEDS TO BE TRUE          WHAT ESCAPE DOES TO IT
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   the lesion is present      ──────►  (i)   THE TARGET CHANGES
   the drug binds it                         a second alteration in the binding
   the pathway is a                          site, or more copies of the target
     dependency                        ──►   answered by: a different molecule
   the drug gets there                             against the same target
                                       ─────────────────────────────────────────
                                       (ii)  THE SIGNAL ARRIVES ANOTHER WAY
                                             a parallel receptor, or a node
                                             below the block, is switched on
                                       ──►   answered by: blocking both, at once
                                                   and not in sequence
                                       ─────────────────────────────────────────
                                       (iii) THE CELL STOPS BEING THAT CELL
                                             the lineage or the histology shifts,
                                             and the dependency goes with it
                                       ──►   answered by: a different class of
                                                   treatment entirely
                                       ─────────────────────────────────────────
                                       (iv)  THE DRUG NEVER GOT THERE
                                             a compartment the agent does not
                                             reach holds viable disease
                                       ──►   answered by: local treatment, or an
                                                   agent with that penetration

   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   AND THE SHAPE OF THE WHOLE THING:

      before treatment     ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░▓      ▓ = the escaping
                           sensitive cells dominate            minority

      on treatment         ░░░░░▓                            the sensitive are
                           the population shrinks              removed FIRST

      at progression        ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓                 what regrows is
                            what was left                      what was left

   Nothing in that sequence required the drug to CREATE anything.  Selection
   and mutagenesis are different claims and only the first one is needed.
```

## What "targeted" commits you to

A targeted agent's effect is **contingent**, and contingent in a strong sense (**mechanism**). It
is not a treatment that works better when the lesion is present and less well when it is absent.
Where the dependency is absent there is no mechanism for it to act through, so no amount of dose,
duration or repetition substitutes. This is the same point the pharmacology answers in this
repository make about an intervention having no route to its target rather than an insufficient
one, and it is the reason biomarker-negative populations are not simply a lower-response subgroup.

Two consequences follow immediately. First, the agent's whole value rests on a test, which is why
the test and the drug are treated as one object — the subject of its own answer in this specialty.
Second, anything that removes the dependency removes the effect entirely rather than blunting it,
which is why three of the four escape classes below are not dose problems.

## Class one: the target changes

The commonest and best-understood route. Under treatment, cells carrying an additional alteration
**in the target itself** are selected — classically one that preserves the target's function while
preventing the drug from binding, and sometimes instead an increase in the amount of target
present (**consensus**).

This is the class with the most actionable answer, because the problem is chemical. A molecule
that binds the altered target, or binds at a different site on it, restores the block; successive
generations of inhibitors against a single target are the direct product of this logic
(**consensus**). It is also the class most likely to be detectable by sequencing rather than
morphology, which is why it is the one a plasma assay can often find.

The same class has a predictable sequel: a drug designed against the second alteration selects for
a third. Each generation narrows the escape space rather than closing it (**mechanism**).

## Class two: the signal arrives by another way

The pathway the drug blocks is rarely the only route to the same output. Escape here is
**activation of a parallel input** — another receptor, or a node downstream of the block — leaving
the drug's target inhibited and irrelevant (**consensus**).

The logical answer is to block both nodes. The practical constraint is not logic but tolerance:
two agents acting on pathways that are also required by normal tissue produce overlapping toxicity
at the dose each needs, and the combination is limited by whichever organ both agents burden
(**mechanism**). This is why combination development is slow even where the biology is obvious,
and why the useful question about a combination is which toxicities it stacks.

It also argues for giving a combination **up front rather than sequentially** where the evidence
supports it: a sequence allows the resistant subpopulation to expand between treatments, while
simultaneous blockade denies it the single step it needed (**mechanism**, with the actual choice
disease-specific and **consensus**).

## Class three: the cell stops being the kind of cell the drug was chosen for

The least intuitive route and the one most often missed. The tumour changes **lineage or
phenotype** — a shift in histology, or a reversible shift in state that carries no new mutation —
and the dependency the drug exploited disappears with it (**consensus**).

Two things follow, and both are practical. The diagnosis is **morphological**, so a plasma assay
can miss it entirely and a tissue biopsy is what establishes it. And the answer is not another
inhibitor of anything: it is a different class of treatment, usually cytotoxic, chosen for the new
histology rather than for the original target (**consensus**).

Worth separating within this class: a non-genetic, reversible tolerant state is a different thing
from a completed histological transformation, and only the first is expected to reverse when the
pressure is removed (**mechanism**). Conflating them is the commonest error here.

## Class four: the drug never got there

Not resistance at all, and the distinction matters. Viable disease in a compartment the agent
penetrates poorly will progress while disease everywhere else stays controlled
(**mechanism**).

The clue is the **pattern** rather than the fact of progression: one site, or one compartment,
advancing while the rest does not. The answer is a different instrument — local treatment to the
progressing site, or an agent whose penetration into that compartment is a property of the
molecule rather than something a higher dose achieves (**consensus**, **country-dependent** in
what is available).

This class is also why **progression is not one event**. Progression confined to one or a few
sites, with everything else controlled, is treated differently from widespread progression in
several diseases: continuing the systemic agent and treating the progressing site locally is an
established option, and continuing an agent beyond radiological progression has disease-specific
evidence behind it rather than being a general rule (**consensus**, strongly
**country-dependent**).

## Why the classification is the point

Progression is an instruction to find out which class this is, because the four answers are
different and three of them cannot be reached by adjusting the dose.

That is the argument for **repeat tissue sampling at progression where the result would change
management**, and for plasma circulating tumour DNA as a complementary route with a different
blind spot: it samples shed material from many sites at once and cannot see a morphological
change, so a negative plasma result at progression is a reason to consider tissue rather than a
reason to stop asking (**consensus**). The population being sampled, and why one biopsy is a
sample of a population under selection, is the subject of the next answer in this specialty.

## The human stakes, said plainly

Everything above is mechanism, and mechanism is the right register for understanding why a drug
stops working. It is not the register for being told that it has.

A deep response to a targeted agent often restores ordinary life quickly and completely enough
that the disease recedes from the foreground. Being told that the scan has changed is therefore
not a gradual disappointment; it is an interruption of something that had started to feel settled,
and it frequently arrives at a routine appointment with no new symptom to explain it. The
mechanistic account on this page — that the population changed, that this was expected, that there
is a next class of answer — is genuinely useful to a clinician and is not comfort.

Repeat biopsy deserves naming too. It is another procedure, with its own risk and its own wait,
offered to someone who has just had bad news, and it is justified by whether the result would
change what is done rather than by completeness. Whether it is the right thing for a particular
person is a conversation, not a protocol, and nothing on this page settles it.

## What an examiner digs into next

* A targeted agent fails after a long response. Name the four classes of explanation and say which
  one a plasma assay is least able to detect.
* Why does a second-generation inhibitor help in one class and not in the other three?
* Why is a combination given simultaneously rather than sequentially, and what limits that?
* Distinguish a reversible tolerant state from a completed lineage change, and say why it matters.
* One site progresses while the rest of the disease is controlled. What does that pattern suggest,
  and what does it not establish?
* Why is "no mechanism against this target" a different statement from "less effective against
  this target"?
* What would make a repeat biopsy at progression not worth doing?

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

The standing documents for this specialty are listed in
[`../../../for-agents/SOURCES-oncology.md`](../../../for-agents/SOURCES-oncology.md). Specific
to this answer:

* The summary of product characteristics or equivalent label for the agent in question, published
  by the licensing authority in your country — for what the agent is licensed against, which test
  defines that population, and what is said about continuing it after progression.
* Your national or regional disease-specific guidance, for whether repeat tissue sampling at
  progression is recommended in that disease, and for whether a plasma assay is accepted as an
  alternative where tissue is not obtainable. These differ between countries.
* Your own institution's molecular tumour board or equivalent pathway, which is the document that
  governs what is tested at progression and who decides.
* A current standard textbook of the specialty, for the escape-mechanism classification itself and
  for the pharmacology of compartment penetration.
* The primary literature, for any particular drug–resistance pairing and for the trials behind
  simultaneous rather than sequential combination, which is where those questions were settled.

## Scope and safety

This is revision material about why targeted agents fail, written for someone already training in
the field. It has had no clinical review. **No drug, gene, disease, dose, response rate or
interval appears here, and none should be inferred** — the licensed indications, the tests that
define them and the options at progression differ between countries and institutions and are
revised frequently; the label and the local pathway in force where you work are the authority, and
this is not. It is not a prescribing guide and not a decision aid, and it describes no
individual's situation. Anyone affected by cancer — their own diagnosis or someone else's — should
be talking to the clinical team looking after that person, who have the imaging, the molecular
results and the history, none of which are here.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The classification is structural and should age well: a contingent drug, a population under
selection, and four ways for the contingency to fail are not facts about any particular era's
drugs. The division between on-target alteration, bypass activation, lineage change and
inadequate penetration has been stable for some time and is how the subject is taught.

Everything attached to it moves. Which escape mechanisms are known in which disease, which of them
have a drug designed against them, whether a combination is given up front, whether plasma
sequencing is accepted in place of tissue, and whether continuing an agent beyond progression is
supported are all disease-specific and are revised on a short cycle, with uneven adoption between
countries. No agent, target or figure is quoted here for exactly that reason: those belong to the
current label and the current guidance rather than to a revision note like this one.

# Kecleon's type changes to the move that just worked, and it only changes when the move worked

Read `AbilityBattleEffects` in the Emerald decompilation, case `ABILITYEFFECT_ON_DAMAGE`, and
**Color Change** is six conditions and one line of consequence.

The conditions: the move was not a no-effect; the move is not Struggle; the move's power field is
non-zero; `TARGET_TURN_DAMAGED` is true, which is a macro testing whether the target's physical or
special damage this turn was non-zero; the target is **not already** of the move's type; and the
target is still standing. If all six hold, `SET_BATTLER_TYPE` writes the move's type into **both**
of the target's type slots and the old identity is gone.

Read the fourth condition again, because it is the whole answer. The type change happens **only
when the hit landed and did damage**. A miss changes nothing. A resisted-to-zero hit changes
nothing. A status move changes nothing. The only hit that produces the new type is the hit that
worked — and once it has, the move that worked is now the move being resisted.

And the capacity was never created by the attack. **Kecleon**'s ability list in Emerald's species
data is `{ABILITY_COLOR_CHANGE, ABILITY_NONE}`: Color Change is the only ability it can have, and
it was in the table before the battle started.

As elsewhere in this specialty: **the objects of study are abilities, lookup tables, damage
branches and reachability lists.** No Pokémon in this answer stands in for a person with cancer or
for a tumour, and the analogy is dropped entirely at the end, where the subject changes.

Clinical claims carry the same marks as the rigorous half: **mechanism**, **definitional**,

closing it (**mechanism**).

The **amplification** variant — more of the target rather than an altered one — has its own exact

The crit itself is instructive about how such a path is bought. `Cmd_critcalc` sums a ladder —

irrelevant. The counter is to block both nodes.

combination is capped by whichever organ both of them burden (**mechanism**). That is why

simultaneous blockade denies it that step (**mechanism**; the actual choice is disease-specific

`CastformDataTypeChange` begins with three identity checks — the species must be **Castform**, the
ability must be **Forecast**, and the battler's HP must be non-zero — and then hands the decision

weather, or no weather, makes it Normal, and Castform's species entry has Normal in both type
slots as its resting state.

Nothing attacked it. **The pressure rewrote the identity**, and this specialty already puts
systemic therapy in the weather.

That is lineage and phenotype change (**consensus**): the tumour's histology or state shifts, and
the dependency the drug exploited goes with it. Two things follow and both are practical. The
diagnosis is **morphological**, so a plasma assay can miss it completely and tissue is what
establishes it. And the answer is not another inhibitor of anything — it is a different class of
treatment, chosen for the new histology rather than for the original target (**consensus**).

The game also marks the distinction that matters most here. **Air Lock** and **Cloud Nine** do not
change Castform's type; they make `WEATHER_HAS_EFFECT` false, and the same routine then returns
Castform to Normal. Remove the pressure and the form reverts. **That is the reversible tolerant
state and not the completed transformation** — a non-genetic, reversible drug-tolerant state is
expected to reverse when the pressure is removed, and a completed histological change is not
(**mechanism**). Conflating the two is the commonest error in this territory, and Castform models
only the first of them. Said plainly, because this is where the analogy would mislead: no mechanic
in the game models an irreversible lineage change, and none is claimed to.

one script at a time:

* **ON_AIR** — Gust and Twister set it conditionally and also set the damage doubling; Thunder and
  Sky Uppercut set it unconditionally with no doubling at all.
* **UNDERGROUND** — **Earthquake**'s hit-everything loop sets it, and Magnitude reaches the same
  loop by a `goto`, which is why the two behave identically here.
* **UNDERWATER** — the generic hit script sets it only after `jumpifnotmove MOVE_SURF`, and the
  trapping script only after `jumpifnotmove MOVE_WHIRLPOOL`. **Surf** and **Whirlpool** are the
  list, and it is two moves long.

Clinically this is not resistance at all, and the distinction matters (**mechanism**). Viable
disease in a compartment the agent penetrates poorly progresses while everything else stays
controlled. The clue is the **pattern** rather than the fact of progression — one site or one
compartment advancing while the rest does not — and the answer is a different instrument: local
treatment to that site, or an agent whose penetration is a property of the molecule rather than
something a larger dose achieves (**consensus**, **country-dependent** in availability).

Which is also why **progression is not one event**. Progression confined to one or a few sites
with everything else controlled is handled differently from widespread progression in several
diseases: continuing the systemic agent and treating the progressing site locally is an
established option, and continuing an agent past radiological progression rests on
disease-specific evidence rather than on a general rule (**consensus**, strongly
**country-dependent**). The emergency answer on mechanism of injury takes the same
semi-invulnerable states apart for the doubling; this answer wants the reachability list instead.

## What the classification is for

Progression is an instruction to find out which of the four this is, because three of them cannot
be reached by changing the dose. That is the case for repeat tissue sampling at progression
**where the result would change management**, and for plasma circulating tumour DNA as a
complementary route with a different blind spot — it samples shed material from many places at
once and cannot see a change of histology, so a negative plasma result at progression is a reason
to consider tissue rather than a reason to stop asking (**consensus**). Why one biopsy is a sample
of a population under selection is the next answer in this specialty.

## Where the metaphor stops

Everything above is abilities, damage branches and a reachability list, and code is a good place
to see them because the conditions are written down. What follows is about people, so it is said
plainly and without the analogy.

A deep response to a targeted agent often restores ordinary life quickly and completely enough
that the disease moves out of the foreground. Being told that the scan has changed is therefore
not a gradual disappointment; it is an interruption of something that had begun to feel settled,
and it frequently arrives at a routine appointment with nothing new to have noticed. The account
above — that the population changed, that this was expected, that there is a next class of answer
— is useful to a clinician and is not comfort.

Repeat biopsy deserves naming too. It is another procedure, with its own risk and its own wait,
offered to someone who has just had bad news, and it is justified by whether the result would
change what is done rather than by completeness. Whether it is right for a particular person is a
conversation, not a protocol, and nothing here settles it.

## What a Gym Leader is listening for

* Color Change fires only when `TARGET_TURN_DAMAGED` is true. What is that condition an analogy
  for, and why is it the most important line in the routine?
* Kecleon's ability list has Color Change in it before the battle starts. Which argument does that
  settle?
* Reflect and Light Screen are tested in different branches of one function. Name the clinical
  claim, and then name what actually limits the answer to it.
* A Critical Hit ignores banked Defense stat stages rather than overwhelming them. Which escape
  mechanism is that the counter to?
* Air Lock returns Castform to Normal. Which distinction does that draw, and which half of it does
  Castform not model?
* Surf and Whirlpool are the entire underwater list. What does the shortness of that list say
  about how a sanctuary site is answered?
* Which of the four routes is a plasma assay least able to detect, and why?

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

The standing documents for this specialty are listed in
[`../../../for-agents/SOURCES-oncology.md`](../../../for-agents/SOURCES-oncology.md). Specific
to this answer:

* The summary of product characteristics or equivalent label for the agent in question, published
  by the licensing authority in your country — for what it is licensed against, which test defines
  that population, and what is said about continuing it after progression.
* Your national or regional disease-specific guidance, for whether repeat tissue sampling at
  progression is recommended in that disease and whether a plasma assay is accepted where tissue
  cannot be obtained. These differ between countries.
* Your own institution's molecular tumour board or equivalent pathway, which governs what is
  tested at progression and who decides.
* A current standard textbook of the specialty, for the escape-mechanism classification and for
  the pharmacology of compartment penetration.
* The primary literature, for any particular drug–resistance pairing and for the trials behind
  simultaneous rather than sequential combination.

The Pokémon side is in the opposite position and is sourced file by file in the closing note.

## Scope and safety

This is revision material about why targeted agents fail, dressed in a game so that the difference
between an altered target and an unused route stays concrete. It has had no clinical review. **No
drug, gene, disease, dose, response rate or interval appears here, and none should be inferred** —
licensed indications, the tests that define them and the options at progression differ between
countries and institutions and are revised frequently; the label and the local pathway in force
where you work are the authority, and this is not. It is not a prescribing guide and not a
decision aid, and it describes no individual's situation. Anyone affected by cancer — their own
diagnosis or someone else's — should be talking to the clinical team looking after that person,
who have the imaging, the molecular results and the history, none of which are here. The analogy
carries contingency, selection and routing only: no part of it stands in for a person or for a
tumour, and none of it says anything about what happens to anybody.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The Pokémon facts are read from the projects' own source, all of it Emerald. Kecleon's species
entry gives types Normal and Normal, an ability list of `{ABILITY_COLOR_CHANGE, ABILITY_NONE}`,
and base Special Defence of one hundred and twenty against base Speed of forty. Color Change sits
in `AbilityBattleEffects` under `ABILITYEFFECT_ON_DAMAGE` and requires, in order: no
`MOVE_RESULT_NO_EFFECT`, the move not being Struggle, a non-zero `power` field,
`TARGET_TURN_DAMAGED` — itself a macro testing `gSpecialStatuses[target].physicalDmg != 0 ||
specialDmg != 0` — the target not already being of the move's type, and non-zero HP;
`SET_BATTLER_TYPE` then assigns the move's type to `types[0]` and `types[1]` both.
`CalculateBaseDamage` lives in `src/pokemon.c` and tests `SIDE_STATUS_REFLECT` in its physical
branch and `SIDE_STATUS_LIGHTSCREEN` in its special branch, each gated on `gCritMultiplier == 1`,
each halving damage or taking two-thirds of it when the battle is double and two defenders are
alive. The same function, on a critical hit, uses the raw Defence when the defender's stat stage
is not below `DEFAULT_STAT_STAGE`, and the raw Attack when the attacker's is not above it.
`IS_TYPE_PHYSICAL` and `IS_TYPE_SPECIAL` in `include/battle.h` are comparisons against
`TYPE_MYSTERY`, which `include/constants/pokemon.h` gives as nine. `Cmd_critcalc` builds its index
from Focus Energy, the high-critical move effects, Scope Lens, and Lucky Punch and Stick with
explicit species comparisons against Chansey and Farfetch'd, indexes `sCriticalHitChance` = `{16,
8, 4, 3, 2}` with `!(Random() % chance)`, and is refused outright by Battle Armor, by Shell Armor,
by `STATUS3_CANT_SCORE_A_CRIT` and in the Wally tutorial and first battle. Flygon's species entry

`WEATHER_HAS_EFFECT` — to Normal; Castform's species entry is Normal and Normal with
`{ABILITY_FORECAST, ABILITY_NONE}`, and the Air Lock and Cloud Nine cases call that same routine
for every battler. `AccuracyCalcHelper` in `src/battle_script_commands.c` tests `STATUS3_ON_AIR`,
then `STATUS3_UNDERGROUND`, then `STATUS3_UNDERWATER`, each skipped only when the matching
`HITMARKER_IGNORE_*` bit is set; in `data/battle_scripts_1.s`, Gust and Twister set the on-air bit

The clinical reasoning is structural and should age well: a contingent drug, a population under
selection, and four ways for the contingency to fail are not facts about any particular era's
drugs. Everything attached to it moves — which escape mechanisms are known in which disease, which
have a drug built against them, whether a combination is given up front, whether plasma sequencing
substitutes for tissue, and whether an agent is continued past progression are all
disease-specific, revised on a short cycle, and unevenly adopted between countries. No agent,
target or clinical figure is quoted here for that reason.

question: In what sense is a single tumour biopsy a sample of a population under selection, and what follows for how a biomarker result is interpreted?
answer_serious:
# One place, one moment, and a population that the next treatment will reshape

A cancer is not a clone. It is a **population** of related cells that have diverged from a common
ancestor, are still diverging, and are under selection — by oxygen, by space, by nutrient supply,
by the immune system and, once treatment starts, by the treatment. A biopsy takes a fragment of
that population from one place at one time.

Three separate consequences follow, and they are usually run together.

* A biomarker result can be a **sampling** result. Finding an alteration establishes that it is
  present in what was examined. Not finding it establishes much less than it is read as
  establishing.
* Variation is **structured**, not noise. It has a spatial shape within a lesion, a different
  shape between lesions, and a historical shape — some alterations are in every cell because they
  were in the ancestor, and others are in a branch.
* Treatment is a **filter**. The population after it is not the population before it, and nothing
  about any individual cell had to change for that to be true.

Each load-bearing claim below is marked with the kind of thing it is: **mechanism** (derivable
from how the biology or the sampling works), **definitional** (true because a classification says
so), **consensus** (widely agreed professional practice), or **country-dependent** (varies by
nation, region or institution, and changes).

## The three axes, drawn

```
   SPACE — within one lesion, and between lesions

      ┌──────────────── one primary ────────────────┐
      │   ░░░░░░░░░   ▒▒▒▒▒▒   ░░░░░   ▓▓▓▓▓        │   a needle takes ONE of
      │   ░░░░░░░░░   ▒▒▒▒▒▒   ░░░░░   ▓▓▓▓▓        │   these regions and the
      │       ▲           ▲                ▲        │   report describes THAT
      └───────┼───────────┼────────────────┼────────┘
              │           │                └── and a metastasis descends
              │           └── a second region          from ONE region, not
              └── the region the needle reached        from the average

   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   TIME — the ancestry, and what is shared because of it

                        ┌── branch ──  ▒▒▒▒  present in SOME cells
      trunk ────────────┤
      present in        └── branch ──  ▓▓▓▓  present in SOME cells
      EVERY cell                         │
                                         └── and two branches may arrive at the
                                             same pathway by different routes

   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   PRESSURE — what a filter does to a composition

      before    ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░▓▓          ░ sensitive   ▓ not
      during    ░░░░▓▓                          the filter removes the ░
      after     ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓              what regrows is the ▓

      NOTHING IN THAT REQUIRED THE FILTER TO CHANGE A SINGLE CELL.
      Selection and mutagenesis are different claims.  Only the first
      is needed to explain the picture, and it is the one with the
      evidence behind it.
```

## Where the structure comes from

Three processes acting together, none of them exotic (**mechanism**).

**Mutation and genomic instability** generate variation continuously. **Selection** acts on it,
and the selective pressures inside a tumour are local: a cell at the hypoxic centre of a nodule is
under different pressure from one at a well-perfused edge, so the two regions are not sampling the
same fitness landscape. **Drift** does the rest, because expanding populations are founded by
small numbers of cells and a founder carries whatever it happened to have.

The result is a **branching** structure rather than a linear sequence of steps, and the branching
has a clinically load-bearing consequence. Alterations present in the common ancestor are in every
cell of the disease; alterations that arose in a branch are in a subset (**definitional**). The
distinction matters because an agent directed at a branch alteration treats part of the disease by
construction, however well the test performed.

Two further features are worth naming. **Convergent evolution** — different regions arriving at
the same pathway through different alterations — means two samples can look genetically unalike
and be functionally alike (**consensus**). And a **metastasis descends from a region**, not from
the average of the primary, which is why discordance between a primary and a metastasis is
expected rather than surprising, with the extent of it disease-specific (**consensus**).

## What one sample can and cannot establish

The asymmetry is the whole of it (**mechanism**):

* **Finding** an alteration establishes that it was present in the material examined, at a level
  the assay could detect.
* **Not finding** one is compatible with absence, with presence below the assay's limit of
  detection, with presence in a region the needle missed, and with a specimen that was inadequate
  for the test.

So a negative biomarker result is only interpretable alongside **what was tested, how much of it
there was, and what the assay can see** — which is why specimen adequacy is part of a molecular
report rather than a preamble to it (**consensus**, with the reporting requirements
**country-dependent**). The limit-of-detection half of that argument is the subject of this
specialty's answer on tumour markers and is not re-derived here; the surface-sampling half is in
the answer on surgical margins.

Repeat sampling improves the evidence and has a cost, which is why multi-region sampling is a
research instrument rather than routine practice, and why the question asked of any repeat biopsy
is whether the result would change management (**consensus**).

## Treatment as a filter

This is the part most often stated as though a drug were mutagenic.

The ordinary account needs only selection. A resistant subpopulation existing at low frequency
before treatment, an agent that removes the sensitive majority, and an expansion of what was left
produces exactly the clinical picture — a deep response followed by progression — with no new
mutation required (**mechanism**). Treatment-induced mutagenesis is a separate claim with separate
and much weaker support, and asserting it where selection suffices is a real error of reasoning.

Three practical consequences (**consensus**):

* **Progression is informative about composition.** What regrew is enriched for whatever survived,
  which is why the mechanism of escape at progression is worth establishing rather than assuming —
  the subject of the previous answer in this specialty.
* **Simultaneous beats sequential**, where the evidence supports it, because a sequence hands the
  surviving subpopulation an uncontested interval to expand in.
* **A pre-treatment result can expire.** A molecular profile obtained before several lines of
  treatment describes a population that has since been filtered, which is the argument for
  re-testing at progression where a current result would change the decision.

## Two instruments, two different blind spots

Tissue and plasma are not ranked, and treating one as a cheaper version of the other is the common
mistake (**mechanism**, **consensus**).

A **tissue biopsy** is spatially specific: it comes from a named lesion, it supports morphological
and immunohistochemical assessment as well as sequencing, and it can therefore establish a change
of histology. Its weakness is that it is one place.

**Circulating tumour DNA** inverts both. It pools shed material from wherever is shedding, so it
can carry alterations no single biopsy would have reached — and it tells you nothing about which
lesion they came from. It depends on shedding, so a low-shedding or low-volume disease can give a
negative result while disease is present. It cannot see morphology at all. And plasma variants are
not all tumour variants: clonal haematopoiesis contributes alterations from blood cells, which is
why plasma results are interpreted with that possibility in mind rather than at face value
(**consensus**).

The honest summary: a negative plasma result is weak evidence of absence, a positive tissue result
is strong evidence of presence somewhere, and neither instrument makes the other redundant. Which
is available, which is funded and which is accepted for a given decision differ markedly between
countries and institutions (**country-dependent**).

## Which lesion, and when

Two questions that follow directly, and are frequently asked badly.

**Which lesion to sample** is decided by what the question is. For establishing a diagnosis, the
most accessible adequate lesion. For a treatment decision at progression, the lesion that is
progressing is usually the informative one, because it is the part of the population that has
escaped (**consensus**). Sampling a controlled site at progression can be an accessible way of
answering a question nobody asked.

**When** is governed by the same test as everything else here: the result has to be capable of
changing what is done. A molecular result that cannot alter management, in a disease where no
matched option exists or is reachable, is a procedure with risk and no decision attached
(**consensus**, strongly **country-dependent**, since what is reachable is a matter of local
availability).

## The human stakes, said plainly

Everything above is population biology and sampling, which is the right register for
understanding a molecular report. It is not the register for being the person the needle goes
into.

A biopsy is an invasive procedure with a wait before it, a wait after it, and a result that may
not be conclusive. Being asked for another one, having had bad news, is a reasonable thing to
decline and a reasonable thing to accept, and the test that justifies the request is whether the
answer would change what is offered — not whether the information would be interesting. That
reasoning should be shared out loud with the person being asked, because it is the reasoning that
makes the request legitimate.

It is also worth being plain that "the result might be a sampling artefact" is a hard sentence to
hear. People are told a test was negative and reasonably take that as a fact about themselves
rather than a fact about a fragment of tissue. The uncertainty described on this page is real, it
is not a hedge, and conveying it without turning a result into a riddle is a skill rather than a
disclaimer. None of the reasoning here determines what will happen to any individual, and no
figure of any kind appears in this answer for that reason.

## What an examiner digs into next

* A biomarker test is negative. List everything that result is compatible with, in order of how
  often it is the explanation.
* Why is an alteration present in every cell a different kind of target from one present in a
  branch?
* Why is discordance between a primary and a metastasis expected rather than an error?
* A deep response is followed by progression. Explain it using selection only, and say what would
  be needed to justify adding mutagenesis to the account.
* Give two things circulating tumour DNA can establish that one biopsy cannot, and two it cannot
  establish at all.
* Why is clonal haematopoiesis a problem specifically for plasma assays?
* At progression, which lesion should be sampled, and what would make the answer different?

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

The standing documents for this specialty are listed in
[`../../../for-agents/SOURCES-oncology.md`](../../../for-agents/SOURCES-oncology.md). Specific
to this answer:

* The molecular reporting standard your laboratory reports against, published by the body that
  maintains it — for what specimen adequacy means for each assay, what is stated about the limit
  of detection, and how a negative result is to be worded. This is the single most useful document
  for this answer.
* Your national or regional guidance on circulating tumour DNA testing in the specific disease,
  for whether it is accepted in place of tissue and for which decisions. This differs sharply
  between countries and is being revised.
* Your own institution's protocol for repeat biopsy at progression, including who authorises it
  and what the specimen requirements are.
* A current standard textbook of the specialty, for clonal evolution, truncal and subclonal
  alterations and convergent evolution as concepts.
* The primary literature, for multi-region sequencing studies, for primary–metastasis discordance
  in a particular disease, and for clonal haematopoiesis as a source of plasma variants — all
  three of which rest on specific studies rather than on mechanism.

## Scope and safety

This is revision material about what a tumour sample is a sample of, written for someone already
training in the field. It has had no clinical review. **No discordance rate, detection limit,
allele fraction or sampling figure appears here, and none should be inferred** — those are
assay-specific and disease-specific, they differ between laboratories and countries, and they are
revised; the reporting standard and local protocol in force where you work are the authority, and
this is not. It is not a reporting guide, not a testing protocol and not a decision aid, and it
describes no individual's specimen or situation. Anyone affected by cancer — their own diagnosis
or someone else's — should be talking to the clinical team looking after that person, who have the
specimen, the report and the history, none of which are here.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The reasoning is structural and will not date. A tumour has always been a population, a biopsy has
always been one sample of it, and the asymmetry between finding something and not finding it
follows from sampling rather than from any current technology.

What moves is everything technological and everything administrative. Assay sensitivity, which
genes are on a panel, whether plasma testing is accepted in place of tissue and for which
decisions, whether multi-region or serial sampling has any routine role, and how a negative result
must be worded in a report are all actively changing and unevenly adopted between countries and
between laboratories in the same country. Clonal haematopoiesis as a confounder is understood as a
mechanism and quantified only study by study. No assay, panel, gene or figure is named here,
deliberately: those belong to the current reporting standard and the current guidance rather than
to a revision note like this one.
